title: Problem memory's bases and summaries move behind the storage interface, so PostgreSQL hosts agree
request: Move the problem memory's Project and Problem bases and its summaries from workspace files into the storage interface, with a PostgreSQL implementation chosen like the other stores, a numbered migration, the file-to-database move and tests on both stores (finding 10 of the problem-memory review).
spec: Files behave and lie on disk as before; on PostgreSQL a revision conflict is still a 409, a summary from an older cursor is never published, a purge leaves a tombstone and never deletes a ledger row, storage migrate copies bases and summaries and verify counts them, and processes racing on one revision leave one winner.
plan: read the storage pattern: Protocols, file and PostgreSQL stores, migrations, migrate and verify
add the memory_base and memory_summary tables in models.py and migration 0024
a MemoryBases store with a file and a PostgreSQL implementation
bases.py and summary.py call the store instead of reading and writing files
migrate copies bases and summaries and verify counts them
tests that run the same contract on files and on PostgreSQL, a process race and a migrate

decisions.decision: A base change is one store call change(scope, scope_id, blank, step): the store reads, runs the step, writes
decisions.why: every rule (revisions, stale marks, idempotency keys) stays in bases.py and the two stores differ only in how they make the read and write one step

decisions.decision: On PostgreSQL a change takes a transaction-scoped advisory lock on the scope, then updates only where the row version is still the one read
decisions.why: the step writes memory items before the base row; a purely optimistic retry would let a losing writer leave its memory item behind, so the step must run once against the current state; the version check still refuses a write whose row moved underneath

decisions.decision: A summary publish is one INSERT ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE WHERE stored cursor <= new cursor
decisions.why: PostgreSQL compares integer arrays in order, as Python compares tuples, so the compare and the swap are one atomic statement on any host

decisions.decision: A purge sets purged_at and a trigger refuses DELETE on memory_base; summaries are still deleted
decisions.why: the owner's rule keeps deleted data in the store; summaries are derived and rebuilt on the next read, as the files were

decisions.decision: A migrated base row's id is made from the workspace and the file's path under memory/bases
decisions.why: a second migrate run inserts nothing, and a live base the database workspace wrote since is kept by the live-scope unique index

change: New dclab_rnd/storage/memory_bases.py (FileMemoryBases, PgMemoryBases, open_memory_bases), the MemoryBases Protocol and open_memory_bases in dclab_rnd/storage/__init__.py, the two tables in dclab_rnd/storage/models.py, migration 0024_memory_bases.py, the bases and summaries step in dclab_rnd/storage/migrate.py (copy and verify), dclab_rnd/memory/bases.py and summary.py on the store, and tests/test_memory_bases_storage.py.

findings.defect: Bases and summaries were always JSON files behind a per-host file lock, even with DCLAB_DATABASE_URL set.
findings.scenario: Two API or worker hosts on one database: an edit on host A is not seen by host B, and both accept expected_revision 0 for the same base.
findings.cause: bases.py and summary.py built paths under the workspace folder and locked with filelock.held
findings.fix: a MemoryBases store chosen like the other stores; on PostgreSQL an advisory lock per scope, a version-checked UPDATE and a conditional summary upsert

findings.defect: The migrate step reported every base as already there although it copied them.
findings.scenario: A first storage migrate of three bases reported copied 0, already 3, while the rows were in the database.
findings.cause: an INSERT ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING's rowcount was not reliable through this driver
findings.fix: the insert returns its key and the copy is counted when a row comes back

findings.defect: A purge could have written an older copy of a base over a newer one.
findings.scenario: A purge selects the live rows, a change on another host commits a new revision, then the purge tombstones the row with the document it read first.
findings.cause: the tombstone was built from the document read before the scope's lock was taken
findings.fix: the purge takes each scope's advisory lock and reads the row again before it writes the tombstone

findings.defect: One test of the existing suite asserts the file layout and fails on PostgreSQL.
findings.scenario: test_problem_memory_active test_summary_cas_rejects_stale_worker_and_purge_clears_vectors_and_summary writes a vector file into memory/ and looks for bases/purged files, which PostgreSQL does not write.
findings.cause: the test reads the workspace folder instead of the store, and does not pin DCLAB_DATABASE_URL to files as the review-fixes tests do
findings.fix: not changed in this package: pin that test to files or check tombstones through open_memory_bases; the same behaviour on PostgreSQL is covered by the new tests
findings.open: the A6 acceptance test of the same file already failed on PostgreSQL before this package (a hard-coded workspace id local)

measurements.name: The package's tests on files and on PostgreSQL
measurements.gate: every listed test file passes on files and with --pg
measurements.result: files: 59 tests in 7 files pass; PostgreSQL: 57 of 59 pass, the two failures are in test_problem_memory_active (one file-layout test, one that failed before the change)
measurements.next: pin the file-layout test to files and fix the A6 test's hard-coded workspace id
limits: the race uses four processes on one machine, not two hosts
the full suite was not run

outcome: Bases and summaries now follow DCLAB_DATABASE_URL like every other store; files are unchanged on disk; on PostgreSQL conflicts, the summary cursor and purges hold across processes, and migrate copies and counts them.
lessons: When a read-modify-write step has side effects outside the row, a lock per scope plus a version check is safer than optimistic retries.
Count inserted rows by what the statement returns, not by rowcount.
risks: Summary docs keep the scope's workspace id in their key, so a summary moved from a folder workspace may simply be rebuilt on first read.
